scenarios.title: The machine that forgot its memory
scenarios.situation: A desktop powers on: fans spin, drives hum, but the screen stays black and you hear three short beeps, repeating.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and what is your first action?
choices: Reseat the RAM modules in their slots
Replace the power supply unit
Flash the motherboard BIOS to the latest version
Replace the CMOS battery
scenarios.why: Repeating short beeps during POST are the firmware's way of reporting a memory fault on most desktop BIOS/UEFI implementations. Power down, unplug, ground yourself, and reseat the RAM so the contacts seat firmly; that single step resolves a large share of no-video boots before any part gets replaced.
scenarios.hint: What does the system check before it ever touches the disk?

scenarios.title: The smell of hot plastic
scenarios.situation: A workstation randomly shuts off under load. Today there is a faint burning-plastic smell from the rear of the case, near the power supply.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct diagnosis and next step?
choices: The PSU is failing — power down, unplug, and replace it
The CPU is overheating — reapply thermal paste immediately while it is hot
The wall outlet is bad — plug the PC into a different circuit and keep working
The OS is corrupt — reinstall Windows before the hardware dies
scenarios.why: A burning smell plus random shutdowns under load points squarely at a failing power supply. Capacitors inside a PSU hold charge even when unplugged, so the safe move is to power down, unplug, and replace the unit — never open a PSU or keep running a machine that smells like it is cooking.
scenarios.hint: Which component converts wall power for every other part — and what do you never open?

scenarios.title: The five-minute boot
scenarios.situation: A user's five-year-old desktop takes five minutes to boot and crawls opening apps. It has a spinning hard drive, 8 GB of RAM, and a healthy CPU.
scenarios.prompt: Which single upgrade gives the biggest real-world speed gain?
choices: Replace the HDD with an NVMe SSD
Add a second 8 GB stick of RAM
Upgrade the CPU to a newer generation
Install a discrete graphics card
scenarios.why: On a machine that is disk-bound, moving from a spinning HDD to an NVMe SSD is the most dramatic upgrade you can make — boot and app-launch times often drop several-fold because storage latency, not CPU or RAM, is the bottleneck. More RAM helps only if memory is actually exhausted, and a faster CPU still waits on the same slow disk.
scenarios.hint: Watch what the machine is actually waiting on during that five-minute boot.

scenarios.title: The stick that will not fit
scenarios.situation: You try to install a DDR4 module into an older motherboard's memory slot. It will not seat no matter how you angle it, and forcing it feels wrong.
scenarios.prompt: What is going on, and what should you do?
choices: The board takes DDR3 — the notch keying differs, so stop and get the correct generation
The slot is dusty — blow it out and press harder until it clicks
The module is upside down — flip it end to end and force it in
The board needs a BIOS update to accept DDR4
scenarios.why: DDR generations are physically keyed: DDR3 (240-pin) and DDR4 (288-pin) put the notch in different positions precisely so you cannot mix them. Forcing a module can crack the board or the stick. The right move is to stop, check the board's supported memory type, and install the correct generation.
scenarios.hint: Why would manufacturers cut that little notch in a different spot each generation?
evidence:
Memory: 4x DDR3 DIMM slots, 240-pin
Max: 32 GB DDR3-1600

scenarios.title: The laptop that quits at 3 p.m.
scenarios.situation: A laptop shuts itself off every afternoon during video calls. The bottom is very hot, the fan sounds strained, and it sits on a soft couch cushion.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the best first fix?
choices: Blocked air vents and dust buildup — clean the vents and use a hard, flat surface
A dying battery — replace the battery immediately
Malware — wipe and reinstall the OS
A failing screen — replace the display assembly
scenarios.why: Thermal shutdown is a protective feature: when heat cannot escape, the system powers off to save itself. A couch cushion seals the intake vents, and dust compounds it. Compressed air through the vents (in short bursts, fan held still) plus a hard flat surface or cooling pad restores airflow — no parts or reinstalls needed.
scenarios.hint: Heat has to go somewhere. Where is it trying to exit?

scenarios.title: The ghost on every page
scenarios.situation: A laser printer leaves a faint repeat of the page image further down each sheet. Users also complain the pages smear when touched right after printing.
scenarios.prompt: Which component is failing, and what safety rule applies while you service it?
choices: The fuser assembly — let it cool and avoid touching it; it runs hot enough to burn
The toner cartridge — shake it and keep printing until it is empty
The paper tray rollers — replace them with bare hands for better grip
The formatter board — reseat it while the printer is plugged in
scenarios.why: Ghosting plus unfused toner means the fuser is not reaching temperature to bond toner to the page. The fuser runs at roughly 200 C (around 400 F), so the safety rule is to power down, let it cool, and handle it carefully. While you are in there, remember toner is a fine particulate — use a mask and never a standard vacuum, which blows it airborne.
scenarios.hint: What melts the toner onto the page — and how hot must it be?

scenarios.title: The carpeted workbench
scenarios.situation: You are about to install RAM and an SSD into a desktop on a carpeted floor, wearing a wool sweater. The parts are still in their anti-static bags.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct ESD-safe procedure?
choices: Ground yourself with a wrist strap to the chassis, work on an anti-static mat, and keep parts bagged until install
Rub the parts on the carpet to discharge them, then install quickly
It is fine — modern parts are immune to static discharge
Touch the wall outlet's hot slot to ground yourself, then proceed
scenarios.why: Electrostatic discharge can silently wound components — the damage may not show up for weeks. The correct practice is to equalize potential: wrist strap clipped to the unpainted chassis (PSU plugged in but switched off, or a grounded mat), parts stay in anti-static bags until the moment of install, and you avoid static-generating clothing and surfaces.
scenarios.hint: The damage is invisible and delayed. What is the cheapest insurance against it?

scenarios.title: The 169.254 address
scenarios.situation: A Windows PC that worked yesterday now has no network access. ipconfig shows an IPv4 address of 169.254.18.44 with no default gateway.
scenarios.prompt: What does that address tell you, and what is the first thing to check?
choices: The PC failed to reach a DHCP server — check the DHCP server, scope, and the link to it
The PC has a static IP conflict — assign a different static address
The subnet mask is wrong — change it to 255.255.0.0
The DNS server is down — point the PC at 8.8.8.8
scenarios.why: 169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA — the address Windows assigns itself when no DHCP server answers. It means the DHCP conversation (Discover/Offer/Request/Ack) never completed. Start at the likely break: is the DHCP server up, is its scope exhausted, and is the physical/logical path between PC and server intact?
scenarios.hint: Who normally hands out addresses on this network — and what happens when they go silent?

scenarios.title: Ping works, the site does not
scenarios.situation: From a workstation you can ping a web server and resolve its name, but the browser times out loading the site. Another server on the same subnet loads fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: A firewall is blocking TCP port 443 to that server
The workstation's IP address is wrong
The Ethernet cable is damaged
The server's power supply has failed
scenarios.why: Ping uses ICMP and DNS uses UDP/TCP 53 — both working proves L3 connectivity and name resolution are fine. HTTPS needs TCP 443 open end to end; a host or network firewall rule blocking 443 to that one server explains the symptom exactly. Check the server's firewall rules and any network ACL in the path.
scenarios.hint: Ping and DNS already passed. Which door does the browser actually knock on?

scenarios.title: The router straight out of the box
scenarios.situation: You are setting up a new SOHO wireless router for a small office. It is currently on factory defaults: admin/admin, open network name, WPS enabled.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct hardening order before anyone connects?
choices: Change the default admin credentials, enable WPA3 (or WPA2-AES), set a strong Wi-Fi passphrase, update firmware
Hide the SSID — that alone secures the network
Enable MAC filtering and skip the passphrase since only known devices connect
Leave defaults so the ISP can remote-manage it if something breaks
scenarios.why: Factory credentials are public knowledge, so changing the admin login comes first; then WPA3 (or WPA2-AES at minimum) with a strong passphrase for the wireless itself; then a firmware update to close known holes. SSID hiding and MAC filtering are trivially bypassed and are not substitutes for encryption.
scenarios.hint: Which of these settings is printed in the manual that everyone on the internet can read?

scenarios.title: The 120-meter run
scenarios.situation: A new office drop was wired with a single 120-meter Cat6 run from the switch to a desk. The link negotiates at 100 Mbps and drops packets; shorter runs in the building are clean at 1 Gbps.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong?
choices: The run exceeds the 100-meter limit for twisted-pair Ethernet — add a switch or re-terminate as two shorter runs
Cat6 cannot do gigabit — replace it with Cat5e
The switch port is bad — replace the switch
The PC's NIC driver is outdated — update it
scenarios.why: Twisted-pair Ethernet (Cat5e/6/6a) is specified to 100 meters including patch cords; beyond that, attenuation and crosstalk corrupt frames, which is exactly the slow-and-lossy symptom here. The fix is architectural — an intermediate switch (or fiber for long runs) — not a driver or a different copper category.
scenarios.hint: What is the one number every copper run has to respect?

scenarios.title: The crowded apartment Wi-Fi
scenarios.situation: In a dense apartment building, a user's 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi is slow every evening. A scan shows a dozen neighboring networks, most on channel 6 — including theirs.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best fix?
choices: Move the network to channel 1 or 11, the non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels
Switch to channel 3 to sit between the neighbors
Turn the transmit power to maximum to drown out neighbors
Disable 5 GHz so all devices use 2.4 GHz
scenarios.why: On 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6, and 11 do not overlap; everything in between interferes with both neighbors. Moving to 1 or 11 escapes the channel-6 crowd. Cranking power just raises the noise floor for everyone, and 5 GHz is actually the cleaner band where available.
scenarios.hint: Which channels can coexist without stepping on each other?

scenarios.title: PC to switch, switch to switch
scenarios.situation: You need to patch a PC to a wall jack (which runs to a switch) and also connect two older switches that lack auto-MDIX uplink ports.
scenarios.prompt: Which cable types are correct?
choices: Straight-through for PC-to-switch; crossover for switch-to-switch on the older hardware
Crossover for everything — it is the universal cable
Straight-through for everything — crossover cables are obsolete
Rollover cables for both connections
scenarios.why: Straight-through (T568B on both ends) connects unlike devices — PC to switch. Older switches without auto-MDIX need a crossover (one end T568A, one T568B) for like-to-like switch links. Modern gear with auto-MDIX accepts either, but knowing the rule matters when the link light stays dark on legacy hardware.
scenarios.hint: Like talks to like with a twist. Which pairs get swapped?

scenarios.title: Reachable by IP, not by name
scenarios.situation: A user can open the company intranet by typing its IP address, but the hostname fails. Other workstations resolve it fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the quickest check?
choices: Stale or corrupt local DNS cache — run ipconfig /flushdns, then verify with nslookup
The intranet server is down
The user's subnet mask is wrong
The Ethernet cable is unplugged
scenarios.why: Reaching the IP proves the network path and server are healthy; only name resolution is broken, and only on this one machine — so the fault is local. A poisoned or stale resolver cache is the classic cause, and ipconfig /flushdns clears it in seconds; nslookup then confirms the resolver answers correctly.
scenarios.hint: The road is open but the signpost is wrong. Where does this PC keep its signposts?

scenarios.title: The update that would not finish
scenarios.situation: After a Windows feature update, a PC reboots over and over before reaching the login screen. The user has unsaved work in their profile.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best recovery sequence?
choices: Boot to the recovery environment, try Startup Repair, then roll back with System Restore
Reinstall Windows immediately — fastest way to a clean state
Open the case and reseat the RAM
Delete the Windows folder from a Linux live USB
scenarios.why: A boot loop after an update is a software problem, so the recovery environment (WinRE) is the right arena: Startup Repair fixes boot files automatically, and System Restore rolls the system back to a pre-update restore point without touching user data. Reinstalling is the last resort, not the first move, when user data is at stake.
scenarios.hint: The hardware did not change — what did? And where does Windows keep its undo button?

scenarios.title: The clicking drive
scenarios.situation: A workstation occasionally freezes, Event Viewer shows disk errors, and some files will not open. The drive is a traditional spinning HDD.
scenarios.prompt: Which command-line tool and switch best addresses file-system and surface errors?
choices: chkdsk with the /r switch — it locates bad sectors and recovers readable information
format with /q for a quick wipe
ipconfig /flushdns to clear the resolver cache
sfc /scannow to repair Windows system files
scenarios.why: chkdsk /r implies /f (fix file-system errors) and adds a surface scan that finds bad sectors and recovers readable data. sfc repairs Windows system files, not the file system itself, and formatting destroys the data you are trying to save. Back up first — a failing drive can die during the scan.
scenarios.hint: The errors are on the platters, not in Windows. Which tool speaks to the disk itself?
evidence:
Source: disk | Event ID: 7
The device, \Device\Harddisk0\DR0, has a bad block.

scenarios.title: The corrupted system file
scenarios.situation: Windows behaves erratically — built-in apps crash, settings pages will not open — but third-party apps run fine and the disk passes diagnostics.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct repair order?
choices: Run sfc /scannow; if it cannot repair, follow with DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
Run chkdsk /r on the system drive
Reinstall every third-party application
Replace the motherboard
scenarios.why: When Windows' own files are corrupt but the disk is healthy, sfc /scannow scans protected system files and replaces bad ones from a cache. If the cache itself is damaged, DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth repairs the component store from Windows Update, after which sfc can succeed. Disk tools and hardware swaps miss the actual layer of the fault.
scenarios.hint: The disk is fine and your apps are fine. What is left standing between them?

scenarios.title: The invisible SSD
scenarios.situation: You installed a brand-new SSD, but it does not appear in File Explorer. It does show up in Disk Management as 'Unknown / Not Initialized'.
scenarios.prompt: What must you do before Windows can use it?
choices: Initialize the disk, create a partition/volume, format it, and assign a drive letter
Run sfc /scannow to detect the new hardware
Move the SSD to a different SATA port until Explorer sees it
Install a new copy of Windows on the old drive
scenarios.why: A new disk has no partition table, so Windows cannot present it as a volume. In Disk Management (or diskpart: list disk, select disk, clean, create partition primary, format, assign) you initialize it, create a volume, format with a file system, and give it a letter or mount point. Only then does File Explorer have anything to show.
scenarios.hint: Explorer shows volumes, not raw disks. What has to exist in between?

scenarios.title: The script that would not run
scenarios.situation: On a Linux workstation you wrote a backup script, backup.sh, but typing ./backup.sh returns 'Permission denied' even though you own the file.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Add execute permission with chmod 755 backup.sh (or chmod +x)
Run it with sudo rm -rf to clear the lock
Change the owner with chown root
Reboot into single-user mode
scenarios.why: Linux executes a file only if the execute bit is set for your user class. New files typically get 644 (rw-r--r--) — readable and writable but not executable. chmod 755 sets rwxr-xr-x: you can run it, everyone can read it, and nobody else can modify it — the standard safe mode for scripts.
scenarios.hint: Read, write, execute — which of the three is the file missing?

scenarios.title: Home to Pro, 32 to 64
scenarios.situation: A department bought Windows 11 Home machines but needs BitLocker and domain join, which require Pro. One machine also still runs 32-bit Windows 10.
scenarios.prompt: Which statements about the upgrade paths are correct?
choices: Home can be edition-upgraded to Pro in place; 32-bit to 64-bit requires a clean install
Both changes happen through Windows Update with no reinstall
Pro features unlock automatically after 30 days on Home
32-bit to 64-bit is a simple in-place upgrade
scenarios.why: Edition upgrades (Home to Pro) are supported in place — you change the product key and the Pro features unlock. Architecture changes are not: moving from 32-bit to 64-bit Windows requires a clean install because the entire OS binary set differs. Knowing which changes are in-place versus clean-install is core A+ OS knowledge.
scenarios.hint: Which change swaps the key, and which swaps every binary on the disk?

scenarios.title: The stale lease
scenarios.situation: A laptop moved from the office to a client's site still shows the office's IP settings and cannot reach anything. The Wi-Fi connects fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest fix from the command line?
choices: ipconfig /release followed by ipconfig /renew to get a fresh lease for this network
ipconfig /flushdns to clear the resolver cache
netstat -ano to list open connections
format the wireless adapter's driver store
scenarios.why: The laptop is holding a DHCP lease from the old network — wrong subnet, wrong gateway, wrong DNS. Releasing drops the stale lease and renewing starts a fresh DORA conversation with the local DHCP server. Flushing DNS would not help because the IP configuration itself is wrong for this network.
scenarios.hint: The address belongs to a network you left an hour ago. How do you hand it back?

scenarios.title: The ransom note on the shared drive
scenarios.situation: Monday morning: files on the shared drive have strange extensions and a README demanding payment in cryptocurrency for the decryption key.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct immediate response?
choices: Isolate affected machines from the network, do not pay, and restore from clean backups
Pay the ransom quickly to minimize downtime
Delete the README files and keep working — the files might recover themselves
Email the note to everyone so they know what is happening
scenarios.why: Ransomware spreads across network shares, so isolation comes first to stop lateral movement. Paying funds crime and frequently buys no working key. The professional recovery path is clean backups — which is exactly why tested, offline backups exist. Report through the incident response channel and preserve evidence.
scenarios.hint: Every minute it stays connected, the blast radius grows. What shrinks it?

scenarios.title: The toolbar that installed itself
scenarios.situation: A workstation is slow, pop-ups appear constantly, and a browser toolbar the user never installed keeps returning after uninstall.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct malware-removal sequence?
choices: Investigate and quarantine, disable System Restore, remediate, scan and update, re-enable System Restore, educate the user
Delete the toolbar, empty the recycle bin, done
Reinstall Windows before investigating anything
Disable the antivirus so it stops conflicting with the toolbar
scenarios.why: The CompTIA best-practice order protects the cleanup itself: quarantine first so the malware cannot spread or phone home, disable System Restore so infected restore points cannot reinfect the machine, remediate and scan, then re-enable protection and create a clean restore point. Skipping the System Restore step is the classic way a 'cleaned' PC gets reinfected.
scenarios.hint: Where could a copy of the infection be hiding that survives your cleanup?

scenarios.title: The invoice attachment
scenarios.situation: A user receives an 'overdue invoice' email with an attachment from a vendor they have never heard of. The sender address is one letter off from a real supplier.
scenarios.prompt: What should the user do?
choices: Do not open the attachment; verify the sender through a known channel and report it
Open the attachment to see what the invoice is for
Forward it to the whole team as a warning
Reply asking for a PDF instead of the ZIP
scenarios.why: This is textbook phishing: urgency plus an unexpected attachment plus a lookalike domain. Opening or replying confirms the address is live and can trigger the payload. The safe play is to verify through a separately known contact method and report it to IT/security so the message can be blocked for everyone.
scenarios.hint: Urgency plus a stranger plus an attachment — what is the email trying to make you skip?

scenarios.title: The coffee-shop network
scenarios.situation: A user needs to check work email from a coffee shop's open Wi-Fi. The network has no password and the login page asks for nothing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safest guidance?
choices: Use the company VPN for all work traffic; avoid sensitive logins on the open network
Open networks are fine as long as the sites use HTTPS
Turn off the firewall to speed up the connection
Share the connection with nearby tables to be polite
scenarios.why: Open Wi-Fi means no encryption at the wireless layer — anyone nearby can sniff unencrypted traffic and run on-path attacks. A VPN encrypts everything from the laptop to the company network, neutralizing the hostile local network. HTTPS helps per-site, but the VPN protects all traffic including background services.
scenarios.hint: No password means no encryption. Who else is listening on this channel?

scenarios.title: The new hire's workstation
scenarios.situation: You are hardening a fresh Windows workstation before handing it to a new employee who will handle customer records.
scenarios.prompt: Which hardening steps belong in the baseline?
choices: Install updates, enable the host firewall, set a screen lock, remove unneeded software, use a standard (non-admin) account
Give the user a local admin account so they are never blocked
Disable Windows Update to avoid surprise reboots
Turn off the firewall because the office router has one
scenarios.why: Hardening is about shrinking attack surface: patched software, host firewall on, automatic screen lock, minimal installed software, and least privilege via a standard account. An always-admin user turns every misclick into a system-wide compromise, and relying solely on the perimeter firewall leaves the host exposed to lateral movement.
scenarios.hint: Every open door you do not need is a door for someone else. Which doors can you close today?

scenarios.title: The shared front-desk login
scenarios.situation: Three shifts share one Windows login at the front desk 'for convenience'. Customer data is accessed from that machine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the problem and the fix?
choices: No accountability and excessive privilege — create individual accounts with least-privilege access
It is fine as long as the password is strong
The problem is speed — add more RAM
Shared logins are required for shift work
scenarios.why: Shared credentials destroy accountability: when something goes wrong, nobody can say who did it, and you cannot revoke one person's access without disrupting everyone. Individual accounts with only the permissions each role needs give you audit trails and clean offboarding. Convenience is not a security control.
scenarios.hint: When something breaks at 2 a.m., which of the three people do you ask?

scenarios.title: The retiring hard drives
scenarios.situation: A clinic is retiring PCs whose drives hold patient records. Someone suggests tossing the drives in the dumpster 'since they are wiped'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct disposition?
choices: Follow a documented data-destruction process — e.g., certified wiping or physical destruction — and keep the certificates
A quick format is enough before disposal
Donate the PCs as-is; the new owners can wipe them
Drill a hole in each drive and throw them in the trash
scenarios.why: A quick format only removes the file table — the data remains recoverable. Regulated data like health records demands verifiable destruction: cryptographic/NIST-appropriate wiping with a certificate, or physical destruction (shredding, crushing) by a certified vendor, with documentation retained. Drilling alone is not a certified process and leaves most platters readable.
scenarios.hint: Format deletes the map, not the territory. What proves the territory is gone?

scenarios.title: The parts cannon
scenarios.situation: A technician's first move on every ticket is to replace parts: new RAM for slow PCs, new drives for boot errors, new cables for network issues. His fix rate is poor and costs are high.
scenarios.prompt: What is he skipping, and why does it matter?
choices: The methodology — identify the problem and establish a theory of probable cause before acting
He needs faster suppliers for parts
He should replace the whole PC instead of individual parts
He needs to skip documentation to save time
scenarios.why: The CompTIA six-step methodology exists precisely to prevent parts-cannon troubleshooting: identify the problem, establish a theory of probable cause, test the theory, plan the action (considering effects), implement or escalate, then verify and document. Theory-first troubleshooting is cheaper, faster, and teaches you the actual fault instead of masking it.
scenarios.hint: What is cheaper than a new part and works before you touch a screwdriver?

scenarios.title: Blue screen after the upgrade
scenarios.situation: Right after a RAM upgrade, a PC throws blue screens under load. It was stable for months before today.
scenarios.prompt: Applying the troubleshooting methodology, what is your theory and first test?
choices: The new RAM is faulty or unseated — revert to the old modules and test stability
Windows is corrupt — reinstall the OS
The power supply is too weak — install a bigger one
The user needs a new PC — quote a replacement
scenarios.why: The methodology says to question the obvious and consider recent changes first: the only thing that changed is the RAM. The cheapest theory-test is to revert to the known-good configuration — reseat or remove the new modules — and observe. If stability returns, you have isolated the fault without spending a dollar.
scenarios.hint: What changed today that did not change yesterday?
evidence:
MEMORY_MANAGEMENT (0x1A)
First seen: today, after RAM install

scenarios.title: The 100% disk
scenarios.situation: A user's PC is painfully slow. Task Manager shows Disk at 100% constantly, with the antivirus and a disk-indexing service at the top.
scenarios.prompt: What is the reasoned next step?
choices: Identify which process is hammering the disk, check drive health, and consider an SSD upgrade if the HDD is the bottleneck
Add more RAM — slowness is always a memory problem
Reinstall Windows immediately
Disable the antivirus permanently
scenarios.why: Task Manager turns a vague 'slow' into a measurable symptom: sustained 100% disk utilization. The next step is to identify the consumer, rule out a failing drive (SMART data, diagnostics), and recognize the pattern — a spinning HDD saturated by background I/O is the classic case where an SSD upgrade transforms the machine. Disabling security software trades safety for speed you could get properly.
scenarios.hint: Slow is a feeling; 100% disk is a fact. What is the disk actually doing?

scenarios.title: No bootable device
scenarios.situation: A desktop that worked Friday now shows 'No bootable device' on Monday. Nothing was installed over the weekend.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct theory-first approach?
choices: Check boot order in firmware and verify the drive is detected and cabled — a dead CMOS battery or loose cable fits the timeline
Reinstall Windows from USB right away
Replace the hard drive — it is definitely dead
Flash the BIOS to the latest version
scenarios.why: 'No bootable device' means the firmware cannot find a boot loader, not necessarily that the drive is dead. Over a weekend, the likely culprits are a CMOS battery losing the boot order, a bumped SATA cable, or a drive that finally failed. Checking firmware detection and cabling first distinguishes a five-minute fix from an unnecessary reinstall.
scenarios.hint: The firmware is telling you what it cannot find. What are the innocent explanations?

scenarios.title: The app that dies on launch
scenarios.situation: One accounting application crashes immediately on launch for a single user. It works for everyone else, and the PC is otherwise healthy.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most efficient troubleshooting path?
choices: Check Event Viewer for the crash details, then repair or reinstall the app and verify the user's profile/data
Reimage the entire PC
Replace the PC's RAM
Reinstall the operating system
scenarios.why: One user, one app, healthy PC — the fault is scoped to the application's installation or that user's profile/data. Event Viewer's application log gives the actual exception instead of guesses, and a repair/reinstall plus a profile check resolves it at the right layer. Reimaging the whole machine for one app's crash is using a sledgehammer on a thumbtack.
scenarios.hint: Who is affected: everyone, or one person and one app? What does that scope tell you?

scenarios.title: The network that blinks
scenarios.situation: A workstation loses network connectivity for a few minutes several times a day, then recovers on its own. Other machines on the same switch are fine.
scenarios.prompt: How do you test a theory here?
choices: Run ping -t to the gateway during an outage, swap the cable and switch port, and check for a duplicate IP
Replace the workstation's motherboard
Reinstall the network printer drivers
Upgrade the building's internet plan
scenarios.why: Intermittent faults demand observation during the failure: a continuous ping to the gateway timestamps exactly when drops happen, and swapping the cable and port isolates the physical path cheaply. A duplicate IP or a flaky cable/NIC fits 'one machine, comes and goes' far better than anything upstream — the switch and ISP are exonerated by the healthy neighbors.
scenarios.hint: You cannot fix what you cannot catch. How do you watch the exact moment it fails?

scenarios.title: The fix nobody wrote down
scenarios.situation: A senior tech resolves a tricky printer issue but closes the ticket with 'fixed it'. Next month the same issue takes another tech three hours.
scenarios.prompt: Which methodology step was skipped, and why does it matter?
choices: Document findings, actions, and outcomes — the final step that turns one fix into organizational knowledge
He should have replaced the printer instead of fixing it
The ticket should have been left open forever
Documentation is the user's job, not the technician's
scenarios.why: Documentation is the explicit final step of the troubleshooting methodology: record the symptoms, the theory, what was tried, and what worked. Without it, every recurrence starts from zero and the organization pays for the same diagnosis twice. A good ticket is a gift to the next technician — who might be future you.
scenarios.hint: Whose three hours could one paragraph have saved?

scenarios.title: The live power supply
scenarios.situation: A junior tech wants to 'save time' by swapping a case fan without powering down, and is not wearing any ESD protection.
scenarios.prompt: What do you tell them?
choices: Power down and unplug first, then use ESD protection — live work risks shock and static damage
It is fine for fans; only the motherboard needs power-off
Speed matters more than procedure on simple jobs
Just touch the case occasionally instead of a wrist strap
scenarios.why: Two safety rules collide here and both say stop: never work inside a powered chassis (shock risk, short risk), and always control ESD when handling components. 'Quick jobs' cause a disproportionate share of injuries and fried parts because the guard is down. Power off, unplug, ground yourself — every time, no exceptions for small parts.
scenarios.hint: What are the two different ways this shortcut can hurt — one to the tech, one to the parts?

scenarios.title: The toner spill
scenarios.situation: A toner cartridge bursts during replacement, covering the printer bay and the tech's hands in fine black powder.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct cleanup?
choices: Wear a mask, use a toner-rated vacuum or damp cloths, wash hands with cold water — never a standard vacuum or hot water
Blow it out with compressed air toward your face to see it better
Use the office's regular vacuum cleaner — fastest option
Wash hands with hot water and keep working
scenarios.why: Toner is a fine particulate: a standard vacuum exhausts it into the air you breathe, and hot water can fuse it to skin. The safe procedure is a mask, a toner-rated (HEPA-filtered) vacuum or damp cloths, and cold water for skin. It is a small moment of care that prevents respiratory irritation.
scenarios.hint: Fine powder plus lungs plus heat — which two everyday tools make this worse?

scenarios.title: The Friday 4 p.m. change
scenarios.situation: A tech plans to update the office router's firmware at 4 p.m. on Friday 'because it is quick', with no written plan and no one else informed.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this plan?
choices: No change management: no documented purpose, scope, risk assessment, rollback plan, or maintenance window
Friday is fine — users are leaving anyway
Firmware updates never cause problems
The only issue is not telling the boss
scenarios.why: Change management exists because 'quick' changes cause the longest outages. A proper change has a stated purpose and scope, an assessment of risk and affected users, a back-out plan, and a scheduled window — typically outside business hours with stakeholders notified. If the firmware bricks the router at 4 p.m. Friday, the office has no network and no plan.
scenarios.hint: If this goes wrong at 4:05, what is the plan at 4:06?

scenarios.title: The curious technician
scenarios.situation: While repairing a laptop, a technician opens the user's email 'just to test the Wi-Fi' and mentions a private message to coworkers later.
scenarios.prompt: Which professional principle is violated?
choices: Respect for privacy and confidentiality — never access user data beyond what the repair requires
There is no violation if the repair succeeded
It is fine as long as the user never finds out
Only managers have to respect privacy
scenarios.why: A repair grants access to someone's digital life; professionalism means touching only what the job requires and treating everything seen as confidential. Browsing email to 'test Wi-Fi' is a privacy violation, and gossiping about it compounds it. Trust is the currency of support work — spend it and you do not get it back.
scenarios.hint: The user handed you the keys to their digital home. What did they not hand you?

scenarios.title: The swollen battery
scenarios.situation: A laptop battery is swollen, pushing the trackpad up. A user asks if they can just toss it in the office trash.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct handling?
choices: Treat it as hazardous: do not puncture or trash it — follow battery recycling/disposal procedures and check the SDS
Puncture it to release the pressure, then trash it
Throw it in the regular trash — it is just a battery
Keep using the laptop; swelling is cosmetic
scenarios.why: Swollen lithium batteries are a fire risk — puncturing or crushing them can cause thermal runaway. They are hazardous waste, not office trash: isolate the device, do not charge or puncture the battery, and route it through proper battery recycling. The Safety Data Sheet (SDS) documents the hazards and handling for exactly this situation.
scenarios.hint: What happens inside a punctured lithium cell — and where does office trash go?

scenarios.title: The one-line ticket
scenarios.situation: A help desk ticket reads: 'computer broken, please fix.' No user name, no asset tag, no symptoms, no urgency.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a ticket actionable, and what do you do with this one?
choices: Contact the reporter to capture who, what device, symptoms, steps to reproduce, and impact — then document it
Close it — vague tickets do not deserve effort
Drive to every office until you find the broken computer
Reimage a random PC and hope
scenarios.why: A ticket is a work order and a legal record: it needs the reporter, the asset, the symptoms, what has been tried, and the business impact for prioritization. The professional move is a quick clarifying contact, not a wild-goose chase or a shrug. Good intake is the cheapest time-saver in support.
scenarios.hint: If you had to hand this ticket to a stranger, what would they need to start?

scenarios.title: The repetitive cleanup
scenarios.situation: Every Monday a tech manually clears temp files and restarts a service on twelve lab PCs — an hour of clicking.
scenarios.prompt: What is the appropriate next step under operational procedures?
choices: Write and test a small script (batch/PowerShell) to automate it, then document and schedule it
Keep doing it manually — automation is risky
Delete the temp folders permanently from each PC
Give every student admin rights so they clean their own PC
scenarios.why: Basic scripting is an A+ operational skill precisely for this: repetitive, well-understood tasks are automation candidates. The procedure is to write the script, test it on one machine first, document what it does, and schedule it — turning an hour of error-prone clicking into a reliable, auditable job.
scenarios.hint: An hour of identical clicks is a script waiting to be born. What do you prove before it touches twelve machines?

lessons.title: Hardware & Mobile Devices — Core concepts
concepts: POST is the firmware's self-test before boot: beep codes and diagnostic LEDs report CPU, RAM, and video faults long before the OS loads — learn what the beeps mean and you diagnose no-video boots in seconds.

RAM generations (DDR3/DDR4/DDR5) are physically keyed and electrically incompatible — the notch position, pin count, and voltage differ, so matching the motherboard's supported type is mandatory, not optional.

Storage hierarchy is about latency: NVMe SSDs on PCIe are orders of magnitude faster than SATA SSDs, which are orders of magnitude faster than spinning HDDs — the storage layer is the most common real-world bottleneck.

The PSU converts wall AC to low-voltage DC for every component; its wattage, connectors (24-pin ATX, 4+4-pin CPU, 6+2-pin PCIe), and efficiency rating must cover the whole build — and you never open one, because capacitors hold charge.
Mobile devices trade serviceability for density: expect sealed batteries, SO-DIMM or soldered RAM, M.2 storage, and thermal designs where blocked vents cause protective shutdowns.
Laser printers fuse toner with heat (the fuser, ~200 C): ghosting and smearing point at the fuser or drum, and toner is a fine particulate demanding a mask and toner-rated cleanup.

example.code:
Board manual: '4x DDR4 DIMM, 288-pin, 1.2V, max 128 GB'
Module in hand: DDR3 240-pin, 1.5V, notch offset left
example.walkthrough: The pin count (288 vs 240), the voltage (1.2V vs 1.5V), and the notch position all disagree — this module cannot go in this board, and the keying exists precisely to stop you. Match generation, pin count, and voltage to the manual before buying or installing.

pitfalls: Common trap: forcing a RAM module that will not seat — if the notch does not align, it is the wrong generation, not a tight slot.
Common trap: opening a PSU to 'check the fuse' — charged capacitors make this a shock hazard; replace, do not repair.
Common trap: diagnosing a slow PC as a CPU problem when Task Manager shows the disk pinned at 100% — the bottleneck is storage.
Common trap: using a standard vacuum on a toner spill — it exhausts fine particulate into the air; use a toner-rated vacuum or damp cloths.

lessons.title: Networking — Core concepts
concepts: TCP/IP addressing has two parts: the network portion (which network) and the host portion (which device), divided by the subnet mask — 192.168.1.10/24 means the first 24 bits are the network.

DHCP automates addressing with the DORA sequence (Discover, Offer, Request, Ack); when no server answers, Windows self-assigns an APIPA address in 169.254.0.0/16 — the universal symptom of DHCP failure.

Memorize the everyday ports: DNS 53, DHCP 67/68, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 20/21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, POP3 110, IMAP 143, SMB 445, RDP 3389, SNMP 161/162, LDAP 389 — the exam and the field both assume them.
Twisted-pair copper (Cat5e/6/6a) is limited to 100 meters; beyond that, attenuation corrupts frames — long runs need an intermediate switch or fiber.

On 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi only channels 1, 6, and 11 are non-overlapping; WPA3 (or WPA2-AES minimum) with a strong passphrase is the baseline, and default router credentials must be changed before anything connects.
T568B on both ends makes a straight-through cable (unlike devices); T568A on one end makes a crossover (like devices on legacy hardware without auto-MDIX).

example.code:
IPv4 Address: 169.254.18.44
Subnet Mask: 255.255.0.0
Default Gateway: (blank)
example.walkthrough: The 169.254.x.x address with no gateway is APIPA — Windows gave up waiting for DHCP. Do not troubleshoot DNS or the application layer; the DHCP conversation never completed, so check the server, the scope, and the path between this PC and it.

pitfalls: Common trap: troubleshooting DNS when the address is APIPA — the problem is a layer below name resolution.
Common trap: assuming a cable fault when ping works but HTTPS fails — ICMP and TCP 443 are different doors; check firewall rules for the port.
Common trap: hiding the SSID as 'security' — it is trivially discovered and no substitute for WPA2/WPA3 encryption.
Common trap: running copper past 100 meters and blaming the switch — physics, not hardware, is the limit.

lessons.title: Operating Systems — Core concepts
concepts: Windows recovery is layered: Startup Repair fixes boot files automatically, System Restore rolls back system state without touching user data, and a full reinstall is the last resort — match the tool to the layer of the fault.

chkdsk repairs the file system and disk surface (/r finds bad sectors and recovers data); sfc /scannow repairs protected Windows system files; DISM repairs the component store sfc draws from — three tools, three different layers.
A new disk is invisible to File Explorer until it is initialized, partitioned, formatted, and assigned a letter or mount point — Explorer shows volumes, not raw disks.
Linux permissions are three triples (owner/group/others) of read-write-execute: 755 (rwxr-xr-x) is the standard safe mode for scripts — you can run it, others can only read it.

Windows edition upgrades (Home to Pro) happen in place via a key change; architecture changes (32-bit to 64-bit) require a clean install — know which transitions are upgrades and which are reinstalls.
The command line is the faster diagnostic path: ipconfig /release and /renew for DHCP, /flushdns for the resolver cache, ping and tracert for connectivity, Task Manager and Event Viewer for behavior.

example.code:
$ ls -la backup.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 tech tech 214 Oct 6 09:12 backup.sh
$ chmod 755 backup.sh
$ ./backup.sh   # now runs
example.walkthrough: The file was 644 — readable and writable but missing the execute bit, so the kernel refused to run it. chmod 755 sets rwxr-xr-x: execute for the owner, read-only for everyone else. Permission denied on a script you own is almost always the missing x bit.

pitfalls: Common trap: running chkdsk when Windows system files are corrupt — chkdsk fixes the disk, sfc fixes Windows; use the right layer.
Common trap: reinstalling Windows for a boot loop caused by a bad update — WinRE's Startup Repair and System Restore exist for exactly this.
Common trap: chmod 777 to 'fix' permissions — it grants everyone full control; 755 is the safe standard for scripts.
Common trap: formatting a drive to fix file-system errors before backing up — chkdsk /r first, and back up before either.

lessons.title: Security — Core concepts
concepts: Malware types differ by behavior: viruses need a host, worms self-propagate, Trojans masquerade as legitimate software, ransomware encrypts for payment, rootkits hide, keyloggers and spyware steal — the type drives the response.

The malware-removal best practice has an order for a reason: investigate and quarantine, disable System Restore (so infected restore points cannot reinfect), remediate, scan and update, re-enable protection, educate the user.
Ransomware response is isolate, do not pay, restore from clean backups — every minute of connectivity grows the blast radius, and payment funds crime with no guarantee of a working key.

Wireless safety starts with encryption: WPA3 (or WPA2-AES) with strong passphrases, default credentials changed, firmware updated; on untrusted open networks, a VPN encrypts all traffic past the hostile airwaves.
Workstation hardening shrinks attack surface: patch promptly, host firewall on, screen lock enforced, unneeded software removed, and users on standard accounts — least privilege everywhere.

Access control fundamentals: individual accounts (accountability), least privilege (minimum necessary access), and proper disposal of drives holding sensitive data (certified wiping or destruction, never just a format).

example.code:
1. Investigate symptoms, quarantine the machine from the network
2. Disable System Restore (purges infected restore points)
3. Remediate: remove the malware with trusted tools
4. Schedule scans + updates; re-enable System Restore, make clean point
5. Educate the user on the infection vector
example.walkthrough: Each step protects the next: quarantine stops spread, disabling System Restore removes the hiding place, remediation cleans, and re-enabling protection plus user education prevents recurrence. Skip step 2 and the 'cleaned' machine reinfects itself from its own restore points.

pitfalls: Common trap: paying the ransom — it funds the attackers and often buys no working decryption.
Common trap: cleaning malware without disabling System Restore first — the infection returns from restore points.
Common trap: trusting a quick format before disposing of drives — formatting removes the file table, not the data; use certified destruction.
Common trap: giving users local admin 'to avoid tickets' — every misclick becomes a system-wide compromise.

lessons.title: Software & Hardware Troubleshooting — Core concepts
concepts: The six-step methodology is the framework: 1) identify the problem, 2) establish a theory of probable cause, 3) test the theory, 4) establish a plan of action and identify potential effects, 5) implement the solution or escalate, 6) verify full functionality, implement preventive measures — and document throughout.
Always question the obvious and check recent changes first: the thing that changed today is the prime suspect for the thing that broke today.
Scope the fault before you act: one user versus everyone, one app versus the whole OS, one machine versus the switch — the scope tells you which layer to work in.
Test theories with the cheapest reversible check first: reseat before replace, revert the change before reinstalling, ping -t during the outage before replacing infrastructure.
Intermittent faults must be observed during failure — continuous monitoring (ping -t, logs, Event Viewer) catches what one-time checks miss.
Documentation is the final step, not optional paperwork: symptoms, theories, actions, and outcomes turn one diagnosis into knowledge the whole team reuses.

example.code:
Symptom: BSODs began today, after a RAM upgrade
Theory: new module faulty or unseated (recent change)
Test: revert to old modules -> stable for 2 hours
Action: replace the new kit; document the stop code and outcome
example.walkthrough: The timeline is the evidence: months of stability, then failure immediately after a change. The methodology says establish that theory first and test it with the cheapest reversible step — reverting the RAM — before spending money or reinstalling anything.

pitfalls: Common trap: the parts cannon — replacing components before establishing a theory; expensive, slow, and teaches nothing.
Common trap: skipping the plan-of-action step — changes without considering effects cause the next outage.
Common trap: declaring victory after the symptom stops — verify full functionality and add the preventive measure, or it recurs.
Common trap: closing tickets with 'fixed it' — undocumented fixes evaporate and the next tech pays for the diagnosis again.

lessons.title: Operational Procedures — Core concepts
concepts: Safety is procedural, not optional: power down and unplug before working inside a chassis, use ESD protection (wrist strap, mat, bagged parts), and never open a PSU — capacitors hold charge.

Environmental controls cover the nasty stuff: toner is a fine particulate (mask, toner-rated vacuum, cold water), swollen lithium batteries are a fire risk (no puncture, recycle as hazardous waste), and the SDS documents every hazard.

Change management turns risky changes into routine ones: documented purpose, scope, risk assessment, rollback plan, and a maintenance window with stakeholders notified — 'quick' unplanned changes cause the longest outages.
Documentation makes work repeatable: tickets need who, what device, symptoms, steps to reproduce, and impact; fixes need findings, actions, and outcomes recorded.
Professionalism is a control: active listening, plain language instead of jargon, respect for privacy (touch only what the repair requires), and honest timelines build the trust support runs on.
Basic scripting multiplies a technician: repetitive, well-understood tasks become tested, documented, scheduled scripts instead of an hour of error-prone clicking.

example.code:
Change request: router firmware update
Purpose: patch CVE in current firmware
Scope: office edge router only
Risk: 10-min outage if reboot needed; brick risk low
Rollback: config backup + previous firmware image on USB
Window: Sat 06:00-07:00, staff notified
example.walkthrough: Every line answers a question the 4 p.m. Friday plan could not: why (purpose), what could break (risk), how to undo it (rollback), and when it is safe (window). Change management is just written-down prudence — and it is what stands between a routine update and a surprise outage.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating ESD as optional on 'quick jobs' — static damage is invisible and delayed, and quick jobs cause a disproportionate share of it.
Common trap: hot water on a toner-covered hands — heat fuses toner to skin; cold water only.
Common trap: browsing user data 'to test' — access beyond the repair's needs is a privacy violation, full stop.
Common trap: automating before testing — run the script on one machine and document it before it touches twelve.

lessons.title: Network triage: from cable to cloud in five commands
concepts: Every network problem lives on a layer. Start at the bottom: is the cable plugged in and the link light on? A lit link light with no connectivity means Layer 1 is fine and the fault is logical — usually addressing, DHCP, or DNS. This bottom-up habit keeps you from reinstalling drivers for a DHCP outage.

`ipconfig /all` is your map. It shows the IPv4 address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers. A 169.254.x.x address with no gateway is APIPA — Windows telling you DHCP failed. A correct-looking 192.168.x.x address with a gateway shifts suspicion to DNS or beyond the LAN.

The ping ladder isolates the fault by climbing outward: `ping 127.0.0.1` tests your own TCP/IP stack; `ping <default-gateway>` tests the LAN; `ping 8.8.8.8` tests internet routing without DNS; `ping google.com` adds DNS to the test. The first step that fails marks the boundary of the problem.

`tracert` (and `pathping`) shows every hop to a destination, so you can see exactly where packets die — inside your network, at the ISP, or at the far end. Rows of asterisks with eventual success usually mean a router that deprioritizes ICMP, not a broken path.

DNS failures masquerade as total outages: everything by IP works, but every name fails. `nslookup google.com` tests resolution directly, and `ipconfig /flushdns` clears a poisoned local cache. If names fail but IPs work, fix DNS — not the NIC.

example.code:
ipconfig /all
ping 127.0.0.1
ping 192.168.1.1
ping 8.8.8.8
ping google.com
tracert 8.8.8.8
nslookup google.com
ipconfig /flushdns
example.walkthrough: Read ipconfig first: confirm you have a real DHCP address and note the gateway. Then climb the ping ladder — loopback, gateway, external IP, hostname — and stop at the first failure, because that step names the broken layer. tracert shows where the path breaks beyond your LAN, nslookup isolates DNS, and flushdns clears a stale resolver cache as a last resort.

pitfalls: A failed ping does not always mean 'down' — many firewalls block ICMP while the service behind them works fine.
Seeing 169.254.x.x and 'fixing' it with a static IP in that range: APIPA never routes, so you have only hidden the DHCP failure.
Asterisks in tracert output are often routers ignoring ICMP, not dead hops — judge by whether the trace completes.
Flushing DNS fixes name resolution only; it does nothing for a DHCP or gateway problem.
lessons.try_it: Open a terminal and run the ping ladder against your own network. Write down your gateway address from ipconfig /all first, then predict which ladder step would fail if your DHCP server died — check your prediction against scenario comptia-a-plus-sc6.

lessons.title: The Windows repair toolkit: sfc, chkdsk, and Safe Mode
concepts: `sfc /scannow` (System File Checker) scans protected Windows system files and replaces corrupt ones from the component store. Run it from an elevated Command Prompt when apps crash, Windows behaves erratically, or updates fail. If sfc reports corruption it cannot fix, `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` repairs the component store itself — then run sfc again.

`chkdsk` checks filesystem integrity: `/f` fixes logical errors, `/r` additionally locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (implying /f). Use it when Event Viewer shows disk errors or files go missing. On a suspect drive, back up data first — a dying disk can fail completely under the scan's stress — and expect `/r` to take hours on large drives.

Safe Mode boots Windows with a minimal driver set, which is the right environment for malware removal and driver troubleshooting: if the problem vanishes in Safe Mode, a third-party driver or startup item is the cause. Reach it via Settings → Recovery → Advanced startup, or `shutdown /r /o` from an elevated prompt.

Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) is the source of truth that separates hardware from software faults. Windows Logs → System records disk, driver, and service errors with timestamps — check it before theorizing, because its entries often name the failing component outright.

System Restore rolls system files and settings back to a restore point without touching personal files — useful for bad driver or update rollouts. It is not a backup and not malware removal: the malware-removal procedure explicitly disables System Restore before remediation so infected restore points cannot re-infect the machine.

example.code:
sfc /scannow
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
chkdsk C: /r
shutdown /r /o /t 0
eventvwr
example.walkthrough: Start elevated: sfc repairs system files, and DISM repairs the store sfc draws from if sfc cannot finish the job. chkdsk /r addresses the disk surface underneath — always before trusting file repairs on a suspect drive. `shutdown /r /o` reboots into the advanced startup menu for Safe Mode or WinRE, and eventvwr opens Event Viewer so you can confirm the fault from the logs instead of guessing.

pitfalls: sfc and DISM require an elevated prompt — without it they fail or report misleading results.
chkdsk /r on a multi-terabyte drive can run for many hours; schedule it, and never run it as the first step on a drive with irreplaceable unbacked-up data.
DISM's /RestoreHealth needs internet access to fetch a healthy image unless you point it at local source media.
System Restore is disabled during malware remediation for a reason — re-enabling it too early can restore the infection.
lessons.try_it: Open Event Viewer on your own machine and read the last 24 hours of the System log. Find one warning or error, note its source and event ID, and decide whether it points at hardware or software — then check your reasoning against scenario comptia-a-plus-sc15.

labs.title: Know your address — ipconfig drill
labs.objective: Use ipconfig to read your IPv4 address, subnet mask, and default gateway, and recognize a healthy DHCP lease versus APIPA.
steps: This lab reworks the Networking practice scenario 'The 169.254 address' into commands you run yourself — same concept, hands-on instead of multiple choice.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: ipconfig — the output lists your network adapters and their IPv4 configuration
Read the IPv4 Address line: if it starts with 169.254, the machine failed to reach DHCP; otherwise note the address and subnet mask
Type exactly: ipconfig /all — the detailed view shows the DHCP server address and the lease obtained/expires times
In your own words, say what the Default Gateway line is for and what a missing gateway would break.

labs.title: Follow the packets — ping and tracert
labs.objective: Verify connectivity layer by layer with ping, then map the path with tracert and read where packets stop.
steps: Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: ping 127.0.0.1 — the loopback test proves your own TCP/IP stack works
Type exactly: ping -n 4 8.8.8.8 — four ICMP echo requests to a public resolver; watch the reply times and packet loss
Type exactly: tracert 8.8.8.8 — each hop prints in order; the last responding hop before timeouts is where the path breaks
Compare: if ping to the gateway works but tracert dies at hop 2, the fault is past your LAN — say in your own words where you would look next.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `ping 127.0.0.1`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "Reply".
In the Terminal tab, run `ping -n 4 8.8.8.8`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "packets".
In the Terminal tab, run `tracert 8.8.8.8`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "hop".

labs.success_message: Lab complete — loopback, gateway, remote: you now test connectivity the way the methodology demands, inside out.

labs.title: Repair the layers — chkdsk and sfc
labs.objective: Run disk and system-file repair tools with the correct switches and explain which layer each tool fixes.
steps: This lab reworks the Operating Systems scenarios 'The clicking drive' and 'The corrupted system file' into commands you run yourself.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: chkdsk C: /r — the surface scan locates bad sectors and recovers readable information (on a real machine this needs a reboot to lock the volume)
Type exactly: sfc /scannow — scans protected Windows system files and replaces corrupt ones from the cache
In your own words, say when you would reach for chkdsk versus sfc — which layer does each repair?

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `chkdsk C: /r`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "CHKDSK".
In the Terminal tab, run `sfc /scannow`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "system".

labs.success_message: Lab complete — disk layer versus OS layer. You now reach for the right repair tool instead of guessing.

labs.title: Own the permissions — Linux ls and chmod
labs.objective: Read Linux permission bits with ls -la and set safe script permissions with chmod.
steps: This lab reworks the Operating Systems scenario 'The script that would not run' into commands you run yourself.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: ls -la — the first column shows the permission bits; find a line starting with -rw-r--r--
Type exactly: chmod 755 backup.sh — sets rwxr-xr-x: executable for you, read-only for everyone else
Type exactly: ls -la — confirm the backup.sh line now starts with -rwxr-xr-x
In your own words, say why 755 is safer than 777 for a script.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `ls -la`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "-rw".
In the Terminal tab, run `chmod 755 backup.sh`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "rwxr-xr-x".

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you read permission bits and set them safely. Permission denied will never be a mystery again.

labs.title: Who is listening — netstat and open ports
labs.objective: List listening ports with netstat, map them to services, and spot a suspicious listener.
steps: Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: netstat -ano — active connections and listening ports with the owning process ID
Find the LISTENING lines: note which local ports are open (expect 135, 445, and others on a Windows lab host)
Match each listening port to a service you know: 445 is SMB, 3389 would be RDP — say in your own words what an unexpected listening port could mean
Type exactly: tasklist — cross-reference a PID from the netstat output to the process name behind it.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `netstat -ano`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "LISTENING".
In the Terminal tab, run `tasklist`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "PID".

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you can see which doors are open on a machine and who opened them. That is the start of real hardening.

labs.title: Isolate a DHCP failure with the ping ladder
labs.objective: Use ipconfig, the ping ladder, and DHCP renewal to prove a workstation's outage is a DHCP failure — not a cable, NIC, or internet problem.
steps: Open the simulated terminal and run `ipconfig`. Record the IPv4 address and note whether a default gateway is present.
Identify the address type: a 169.254.x.x address with no gateway is APIPA — Windows self-assigned because DHCP failed.
Run `ping 127.0.0.1` to verify the local TCP/IP stack is healthy independent of the network.
Run `ping 192.168.1.1` (the gateway) to test LAN reachability.
Force a fresh DHCP request with `ipconfig /release` followed by `ipconfig /renew`.
Run `ipconfig` again and document the before/after addresses plus your conclusion: DHCP failure, and whether the renew fixed it.

checks.hint: Run ipconfig and look for the APIPA address that proves DHCP failed.
Ping the loopback address (127.0.0.1) to verify the local TCP/IP stack.
Renew the DHCP lease with ipconfig /renew, then re-check the address.

labs.title: Repair system files and check disk health
labs.objective: Diagnose a crash-prone Windows machine from its event logs, then apply sfc and chkdsk in the correct order.
steps: Open the simulated terminal and launch Event Viewer with `eventvwr`.
Navigate to Windows Logs → System and look for repeated entries from the Disk source — these indicate hardware-level disk errors.
Open an elevated Command Prompt (right-click → Run as administrator) — sfc and chkdsk both require elevation.
Back up critical data first (simulated with `robocopy C:\Users\Tech\Documents D:\Backup /E`), because a suspect disk can fail under scan stress.
Run `chkdsk C: /r` to locate bad sectors and recover readable data — the disk surface must be addressed before file repairs.
Run `sfc /scannow` to repair protected Windows system files onto the now-stable disk.
Document your conclusion: whether the disk errors persist after chkdsk, and whether drive replacement is warranted.

checks.hint: Launch Event Viewer with eventvwr and open Windows Logs → System.
Run chkdsk with the /r flag on the system volume before touching system files.
Run sfc /scannow from the elevated prompt after chkdsk completes.

simulations.title: The PC that will not POST
simulations.brief: A design workstation went dark overnight. The user has a client deadline at noon. Work the evidence in order — theory first, parts cannon never.

steps.symptom: Pressing power: fans spin, drives hum, screen stays black. Three short beeps repeat.
evidence:
3 short beeps, repeating
No video output
No USB power to keyboard
options: Order a new motherboard — beeps mean board failure
Power down, unplug, ground yourself, and reseat the RAM modules
Flash the BIOS from a USB stick
Replace the CMOS battery
steps.explain: Repeating short beeps are the firmware's memory-fault report. Reseating is the cheapest reversible test of the top theory — and it fits the six-step methodology: theory of probable cause first, action second.

steps.symptom: After reseating, the machine boots — then blue-screens under load with MEMORY_MANAGEMENT.
options: Reinstall Windows to fix the memory manager
Test one RAM stick at a time to isolate the faulty module
Increase the page file to 64 GB
Replace the power supply
steps.explain: Booting but crashing under load points at a marginal stick that reseating could not save. Testing modules individually isolates the faulty one — the classic divide-and-conquer move — instead of replacing the whole kit or blaming software.

steps.symptom: One stick fails consistently in every slot; the other three pass. The workstation is stable on three sticks.
evidence:
Stick 3: errors at 0x4F2A1000 (all slots)
Sticks 1, 2, 4: clean
options: Keep running on three sticks and say nothing
Replace the faulty stick with a matching module, verify stability, and document the stop code and outcome
Flash the BIOS — memory errors are always firmware
Overclock the remaining sticks to make up the capacity
steps.explain: Replace with a matching module so timings and capacity stay correct, verify full functionality under load, and document — the final methodology step. Quietly running degraded robs the user of RAM they paid for and hides the incident from the record.

simulations.debrief: You practiced the full loop: decode the POST evidence, form the cheapest theory, isolate by halves, replace precisely, and document. That is the methodology working.

simulations.title: The office with no internet
simulations.brief: Half the office cannot reach the internet this morning; the other half is fine. The ISP says their side is up. Scope the fault before you act.

steps.symptom: Affected PCs show 169.254.x.x addresses; unaffected PCs have normal 10.0.5.x leases.
options: Reinstall the network drivers on every affected PC
Check the DHCP server at 10.0.5.10 — scope exhaustion or a dead service fits the split
Call the ISP — half the office proves it is their fault
Replace the core switch
steps.explain: APIPA on exactly the machines that lost their lease, while others hold valid leases, scopes the fault to DHCP: an exhausted scope or a stopped service. The healthy machines exonerate the ISP, the switch, and the cabling in one stroke.

steps.symptom: The DHCP service is running, but the scope shows 0 free addresses — 250 leases for 250 addresses, many to devices that left weeks ago.
evidence:
Scope 10.0.5.0/24: 250/250 leased
Oldest active lease: 41 days
Lease duration: 30 days
options: Delete all leases immediately — fastest way to free addresses
Shorten the lease duration, reconcile stale leases, and expand the scope or add a second one
Assign static IPs to every affected PC
Reboot the DHCP server and hope
steps.explain: The scope is exhausted by stale leases held far too long. Shortening lease duration lets dead leases expire naturally, reconciling frees the ghosts, and expanding the scope prevents recurrence. Mass-deleting leases can collide with devices still using them.

steps.symptom: After scope cleanup and a shorter lease, affected PCs get 10.0.5.x addresses on renew and reach the internet.
options: Close the ticket — it works now
Verify a sample of previously affected PCs, confirm no duplicates, and document the scope change and new lease policy
Extend the lease back to 30 days to reduce DHCP traffic
Disable DHCP and go all-static
steps.explain: Verify full functionality on a sample, check for duplicate IPs from the outage window, and document the new lease duration and scope size — the methodology's final steps. Without documentation, the next admin re-extends the lease and the outage returns.

simulations.debrief: You scoped by symptom split, read APIPA for what it is, fixed the exhaustion at its cause, and closed with verification and documentation.

simulations.title: The ransomware morning
simulations.brief: Files on the shared drive are renaming themselves with odd extensions and a ransom note appeared. You are the first tech on scene.

steps.symptom: Ransom note on the shared drive; several workstations show the same note on their desktops.
evidence:
Your files are encrypted. Pay 2 BTC within 72 hours.
Do not turn off your computer.
options: Pay immediately to minimize downtime
Isolate affected machines from the network (unplug/disable NICs) and escalate through the incident response channel
Delete the ransom notes and keep working
Forward the note to all staff as a warning
steps.explain: Isolation is the first move — every connected minute lets ransomware encrypt more shares and spread laterally. Paying funds crime with no guarantee, and deleting notes destroys evidence. Escalate: ransomware is an incident, not a ticket.

steps.symptom: Three workstations isolated. One user's PC shows the initial phishing email with a macro-enabled attachment opened at 8:02 a.m.
evidence:
08:02 invoice.docm opened by user
08:20 first encrypted share write
options: Wipe the three PCs and restore them from the last clean backup after confirming backup integrity
Run antivirus scans and return the PCs to service
Restore from the most recent backup without checking it
Decrypt the files with a free tool found online
steps.explain: Confirmed ransomware means the OS cannot be trusted — nuke from orbit: wipe and rebuild from known-clean media, then restore data from backups whose integrity you verify first (backups can be encrypted too). Antivirus on a compromised OS is wishful thinking.

steps.symptom: PCs rebuilt, data restored from verified clean backups, shares back online. The phishing email vector is confirmed.
evidence:
Offline backup from Friday: integrity OK
No encryption markers in backup set
options: Close the incident — systems are up
Verify full functionality, confirm offline backups are current and tested, brief users on the phishing vector, and document the timeline
Delete the offline backups to save space
Keep the details quiet so users do not worry
steps.explain: Recovery is not closure: verify everything works, prove the offline backups that saved you are current and tested, educate users on the exact lure that started it, and document the timeline for lessons learned. Silence just preserves the vulnerability that let the phish succeed.

simulations.debrief: You ran an incident, not a repair: isolate, verify clean recovery media, rebuild, educate, document. That discipline is what separates technicians from incident responders.

foundations.why_needed: A+ is a hardware-first certification: components, connectors, memory types, storage, printers, and mobile devices. This track builds the physical vocabulary the drills assume.
A+ technicians live in the command line: ipconfig, ping, chkdsk, sfc, diskpart on Windows and ls, chmod, ps, grep on Linux. This track makes the Terminal tab feel like home before the missions begin.
